title: Ophthalmic (Eye Drop / Ointment) Administration
summary: Correctly instilling eye drops and ophthalmic ointments to the conjunctival sac.
steps: Verify the medication: correct eye (OD=right, OS=left, OU=both), dose, and frequency.
Perform hand hygiene and don gloves.
Position patient supine or with head tilted back.
Instruct patient to look UP.
With non-dominant hand, gently pull the lower lid downward to expose the conjunctival sac.
EYE DROPS: hold bottle 1–2 cm above the eye. Instill prescribed number of drops into the LOWER conjunctival sac — NOT directly on the cornea.
OINTMENT: squeeze a thin ribbon (0.5–1 cm) into the lower conjunctival sac from inner to outer canthus.
Instruct patient to close eyes gently for 1–2 minutes — do NOT squeeze tight.
Apply nasolacrimal occlusion (gentle pressure on inner corner of eye for 1–2 minutes) to reduce systemic absorption.
If multiple drops ordered: wait 5 minutes between different drops.
Eye drops before ointment when both are ordered (ointment seals the drops in).
safetyTips: Never touch the dropper tip to the eye or eyelashes — causes contamination of the entire bottle.
Nasolacrimal occlusion reduces systemic absorption of beta-blockers and other drops — always apply.
Ointment causes temporary blurred vision — administer at bedtime when possible.
documentation: Number of drops or ointment length

title: Otic (Ear Drop) Administration
summary: Correctly instilling ear drops to treat external otitis, cerumen impaction, or infection.
equipment: Warm water basin for warming drops
steps: Verify order: correct ear (AD=right, AS=left, AU=both), dose, and temperature.
Warm drops to body temperature: hold bottle in hands for 2–3 minutes OR place in warm water. NEVER administer cold drops directly — can cause vertigo.
Perform hand hygiene and don gloves.
Position patient: affected ear facing upward (side-lying or head tilted).
ADULT/CHILD >3 years: pull the pinna UP and BACK to straighten the ear canal.
CHILD <3 years: pull the pinna DOWN and BACK.
Hold dropper above the ear canal. Instill prescribed number of drops along the EAR CANAL WALL (not directly on the drum).
Instruct patient to remain with ear facing up for 5 minutes.
Gently insert a cotton ball if ordered (not pushed deep).
Assess for relief or adverse effects (worsening pain, vertigo, discharge).
safetyTips: Contraindicated in perforated tympanic membrane UNLESS the medication is specifically approved for perforated TM (check order).
Cold drops cause caloric stimulation of the vestibular system — always warm first.
Different techniques for adults vs. children <3 years — pulling direction is opposite.
keyTakeaways: Adult: pull pinna up and back

title: Rectal Suppository Administration
summary: Inserting a rectal suppository for systemic medication delivery, constipation, or local treatment.
steps: Verify order and consent. Assess for contraindications: rectal surgery, rectal or anal bleeding, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, or low platelet count (rectal manipulation risk).
Explain procedure and provide privacy.
Position patient in Sims' position (left lateral with right knee flexed) — this straightens the sigmoid colon.
Don gloves. Unwrap suppository. Apply water-soluble lubricant to the rounded end.
Ask patient to breathe slowly through the mouth (relaxes external sphincter).
With non-dominant hand: separate the buttocks.
With dominant hand: insert suppository rounded end FIRST, directing it toward the umbilicus (not straight in).
Advance 2–4 cm (1–1.5 inches) in adults beyond the internal sphincter.
Hold buttocks together for 15–30 seconds to prevent expulsion.
Instruct patient to retain for appropriate time: laxative suppository − 15–60 min; medication − per drug instructions.
Assist with hygiene. Note suppository retention and any stool passed.
safetyTips: Do NOT administer rectal suppositories in patients with recent rectal/anal surgery, active rectal bleeding, or absolute neutropenia.
Must pass beyond the internal sphincter to be retained and absorbed.
Direct toward the umbilicus to follow the bowel anatomy — not straight posteriorly.
keyTakeaways: Insert rounded end first, toward umbilicus

title: Unfractionated Heparin (UFH) Infusion Titration
summary: Managing an IV heparin infusion using a weight-based titration protocol and aPTT monitoring.
steps: Heparin is a HIGH-ALERT medication. Require two-nurse check for dose, rate, and pump settings.
Obtain baseline aPTT and weight before initiating.
Loading dose per protocol (if ordered): typically 80 units/kg IV bolus (max per protocol). Two-nurse check before administering.
Start maintenance infusion per weight-based protocol (typically 18 units/kg/hr starting rate, capped at protocol maximum).
Check aPTT 6 hours after initiation and after EVERY rate change.
TARGET aPTT: 60–100 seconds (1.5–2.5× normal; verify facility protocol).
TITRATE per protocol:
aPTT <40: bolus + increase rate.
aPTT 40–49: small increase in rate.
aPTT 50–100: no change (therapeutic).
aPTT 101–120: decrease rate.
aPTT >120: STOP infusion for 1 hour, then restart at reduced rate. Notify provider.
Monitor for bleeding: neuro checks (headache, mental status), hematuria, guaiac stools, IV sites, bruising.
Antidote: protamine sulfate. Have available for major bleeding events.
safetyTips: Heparin is a HIGH-ALERT drug. Two-nurse independent check every time dose is changed.
aPTT >120 with symptoms of bleeding = notify provider STAT. Stop infusion.
HIT (Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia): platelet drop >50% after heparin start — STOP heparin, notify provider.
documentation: Infusion rate changes and reason (aPTT value)

title: Insulin Infusion (Regular Insulin Drip) Management
summary: Managing a continuous IV regular insulin infusion using a bedside glucose protocol.
steps: Insulin infusions are HIGH-ALERT medications. Require independent two-nurse check.
Verify: concentration is correct (typical: 1 unit/mL in NS), patient name, blood glucose target per protocol (ICU: 140–180 mg/dL; surgical: 140–200 mg/dL).
Check blood glucose per protocol (typically hourly when initiating or changing rates, then q2h once stable).
Keep D50W at bedside for hypoglycemia.
TITRATE per facility insulin protocol based on current glucose and rate of change.
HYPOGLYCEMIA protocol (glucose <70 mg/dL):
STOP insulin infusion.
If alert and able to swallow: 15–20g fast-acting glucose PO.
If altered or unable to swallow: D50W 25g (50mL) IV push.
Recheck glucose in 15 minutes. Repeat if still <70.
Do NOT restart infusion until glucose >100 and stable.
Avoid interrupting glucose (tube feeding, TPN) without adjusting insulin accordingly.
Transition to SQ insulin before discontinuing infusion (overlap 1–2 hours per protocol).
safetyTips: Insulin is the most common medication associated with adverse drug events. Two-nurse checks are mandatory.
Hypoglycemia is the primary risk. D50W must be at the bedside before starting the infusion.
Abrupt discontinuation of enteral nutrition or TPN without adjusting insulin = rebound hypoglycemia.
